nodes.label: Vannevar Bush
nodes.desc: Imagined the Memex in 1945. In "As We May Think" he envisioned a system where knowledge is navigated by association rather than hierarchy. The first conceptual architecture of the web.

nodes.label: Ted Nelson
nodes.desc: Coined the term "hypertext" in 1963. Designed Xanadu, a universal linking system never completed. Berners-Lee's web inherits his vision.

nodes.label: Tim Berners-Lee
nodes.desc: Invented the World Wide Web in 1989, proposed the Semantic Web in 1998, launched the Solid Protocol in 2016. The architect of the open web.

nodes.label: James Hendler
nodes.desc: Co-author of the Semantic Web manifesto in Scientific American (2001). Contributed to defining RDF and OWL as W3C standards.

nodes.label: Shoshana Zuboff
nodes.desc: In "The Age of Surveillance Capitalism" (2019) she analyses how human data became raw material for economic systems operating without individual consent.

nodes.label: Denny Vrandecic
nodes.desc: Founder of Wikidata, the Wikimedia Foundation's open knowledge graph. Built the infrastructure that makes over 100 million entities verifiable.

nodes.label: Memex
nodes.desc: Device imagined by Bush in 1945. Non-linear, associative, personal. Never built, but it inspired everything that followed: hypertext, the web, knowledge graphs.

nodes.label: Hypertext
nodes.desc: Non-linear text with links between documents. The fundamental principle of the web: not a sequence but a network of relationships between content.

nodes.label: World Wide Web
nodes.desc: System of hypertext documents on the internet. Created at CERN in 1989. Transformed global communication but also enabled concentration of power over data.

nodes.label: Semantic Web
nodes.desc: Extension of the web proposed by Berners-Lee: data has formal meaning readable by machines. The vision was never fully realised, but its standards are the foundation of AI readiness.

nodes.label: Linked Data
nodes.desc: Principles defined by Berners-Lee in 2006: use stable URIs, publish data in RDF, link to external data. The practical grammar of the Semantic Web.

nodes.label: Knowledge Graph
nodes.desc: Graph of verifiable entities and relations. Introduced by Google in 2012. Today it's the structure that powers AI systems when they cite verifiable facts about people and organisations.

nodes.label: Entity Linking
nodes.desc: The process of resolving entity mentions in text to their corresponding nodes in a knowledge base (such as Wikidata). Crucial for machine comprehension and AI search.

nodes.label: Data Sovereignty
nodes.desc: Principle that data belongs to those who produce it. A response to surveillance capitalism. Realised through the Solid Protocol and semantic narrative governance.

nodes.label: AI Readiness
nodes.desc: Capacity of an entity to be read, cited, and represented accurately by AI systems. Built with JSON-LD, Wikidata, and verifiable knowledge graphs.

nodes.label: RDF
nodes.desc: Resource Description Framework. W3C standard from 1999. Represents knowledge as subject-predicate-object triples. The formal language of the Semantic Web.

nodes.label: JSON-LD
nodes.desc: Serialisation of Linked Data in JSON. W3C standard since 2014. The most practical way to implement structured data readable by AI systems on any website.

nodes.label: Schema.org
nodes.desc: Shared vocabulary for structured markup. Created by Google, Microsoft, Yahoo, and Yandex in 2011. Defines the entity types recognised by AI systems.

nodes.label: Solid Protocol
nodes.desc: Protocol proposed by Berners-Lee. Stores data in personal Pods controlled by the individual. The technical implementation of data sovereignty.

nodes.label: RAG
nodes.desc: Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Enhances LLMs by connecting them to external structured knowledge bases. Requires verifiable, well-organised data to work without hallucinations.

nodes.label: Wikidata
nodes.desc: The Wikimedia Foundation's open knowledge graph. Over 100 million entities with unique identifiers (Q-IDs). The most verifiable source for semantic identity.

nodes.label: LLM
nodes.desc: Language models trained on vast amounts of text: ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude. The quality of their representation of an entity depends on the structure of available data.

nodes.label: Surveillance Capitalism
nodes.desc: Economic system that extracts value from human behavioural data without consent. Zuboff's concept: the commercial web as a machine for predicting and modifying behaviour.
